annotations.title: Woe to thee o land, whose King is a child.
annotations.text: [1] S. Jerome (as in most part of his commentaries upon this book) expoundeth this passage in two senses: first according to the simple first appearance of the letter; and mystically concerning the Church. The wiseman seemeth indeed (saith he) to reprove the principality of young men, and to condemn luxurious judges; for that in the one by want of age is infirm wisdom, in the other, mature age is weakened by delicacies. [2] And contrariwise he approveth a Prince of good parts, & liberal education; & commandeth those Judges, which do not prefer voluptuousness before public affairs: but after great labour and administration of the commonwealth, are constrained as by necessity to take meat. Yet to me (saith this great Doctor) something more sacred seemeth to lie hid in the letter: that in Scripture they are called young men, who forsake old authority, and contemn ancient precepts of forefathers; who neglecting God's commandment, desire to establish traditions of men. Which touching points, our Lord threatened Israel by Isaias, [3] [4] for this people hath refused the water of Silo, that runneth with softness, and runneth forth among the old fashioned, choosing rather the streams of Samaria, and gulfs of Damascus, I will give young men to be their Princes, and deluders shall rule over them. Read Daniel: [5] Thou shalt find God ancient of days. Read the Apocalypse of S. John: [6] Thou shalt find that honour, and gravity was reputed in his wisdom, [7] was forbid to call himself a child. Woe therefore to the land, which is king is the devil, who always coveting novelties, rebelled in Absalom against the father. [8] Woe to that land whose Judges and princes love the pleasures of this world. Who, one with a death sentence, say: Let us eat: for tomorrow we shall die. Contrariwise blessed is the land of the Church, whose King is Christ, the Son of the freeborn, descending from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the stock of Prophets, and of all Saints, over whom sin ruled not: and for that cause they were truly free: of whom was born the holy Virgin Mary more free: [9] having no shrub, no branch out of the side, but the whole fruit sprung forth into flower: saying in the Canticles: I am the flower of the field, [10] the lily of the valleys. The Princes also of this land are the Apostles, and all Saints, who have their King the son of the freeborn, the son of the freemen, not of the bondwoman Agar, sons of the freedom of Sara. Neither do they eat in the morning, nor quickly. For they seek not pleasure in this present world; but shall eat in their due time, when the time of reward shall come, and they shall eat in fortitude, and not in confusion. All the good of this present world is confusion: but of the future world is perpetual fortitude. Thus far S. Jerome whose discourse we have here cited at large for a taste of his profound exposition of this book; that such as have opportunity, may read the rest in the author himself. To. 7.

notes.text: This text, and many others, have two senses.
In Kings and all superiors are required mature age, & diligent care of the common good.
Antiquity in matter of faith and religion is to be followed, not novelty.
Also mortification and labour is required in Pastors, not delicacy nor ease.
The B. Virgin Mary more free from sin than the Patriarchs.
